author: willhea
body:
## Related issue

Closes #364

## What does this change?

Splits the single sequential `test` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` into seven
independent jobs plus an aggregator. The old workflow ran every check as a step of one
job (lint, format, fast tests, browser tests, external validation, corpus gates,
packaging gate, remaining slow suites), so a contributor's wait was the sum of all of
them. The seven leaf jobs now run concurrently and the critical path is the longest one.

The seven leaf jobs map one-to-one onto the old steps, deliberately: #364 notes that
regrouping which modules run together would change the skip surface each pytest session
sees, and the `ALLOWED_CI_SLOW_SKIPS` ceiling in `tests/conftest.py` is per session.
Keeping the groupings intact avoids that question rather than answering it.

`lint-format` runs once because lint and format are interpreter-independent. The other
six keep the four-way Python matrix, `fail-fast: false`, and `UV_PYTHON` pinning.

## The required check

Branch protection asks for a context named exactly `test`. Matrix jobs report per-leg
contexts (`fast-tests (3.12)`), so the name had to survive the split. A `test` job that
needs all seven, runs under `if: always()`, and exits non-zero unless every result is
`success` reports that context regardless of how the matrix is later renamed or resized,
with no branch-protection edit.

## Rebased onto develop

This branch was rebased onto `develop` (`2e3fd1c`) rather than merged, so its four commits
sit directly on the integration branch and the pull request contains only its own work.
The rebase was clean, no conflicts.

It was not a formality. `develop` had moved eleven commits ahead, and #599 added
`--run-browser` to the browser step in the meantime; that flag makes a Chromium launch
failure raise rather than skip. The rebase carried it into the new `browser-tests` job
along with its comment, which the collection check below confirms rather than assumes.
The workflow diff against `develop` removes no pytest, ruff or playwright command.

The SHAs and run IDs below are pre-rebase where noted. The runs remain readable, but those
commits are no longer on the branch.

## Measured wall clock

| | SHA | Run | Event | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before | `2e3fd1c` | [31545043740](https://github.com/AgoraDMV/DeltaTrack/actions/runs/31545043740) | push on `develop` | 23:04:37 → 23:10:47 = **6m10s** |
| After | `a59ba18` | [31547783954](https://github.com/AgoraDMV/DeltaTrack/actions/runs/31547783954) | pull_request | 23:47:05 → 23:51:08 = **4m03s** |
| After | `7e578a9` | [31557217880](https://github.com/AgoraDMV/DeltaTrack/actions/runs/31557217880) | pull_request | 02:32:55 → 02:37:07 = **4m12s** |
| After | `bc1ad7f` | [31562459981](https://github.com/AgoraDMV/DeltaTrack/actions/runs/31562459981) | pull_request | 04:11:37 → 04:16:37 = **5m00s** |

Between **1m10s and 2m07s** off the wall clock, across three post-split runs. Read as
total workflow duration rather than any single job's, since a split moves time between
jobs rather than removing it.

The spread across those three runs (4m03s, 4m12s, 5m00s) is larger than it looks from any
one of them, and only one baseline run was measured, so the honest claim is a saving of
roughly one to two minutes rather than a single figure. Hosted-runner variance and how
quickly seven concurrent jobs get scheduled both feed into it. Quoting the best pair
(6m10s against 4m03s) would overstate the typical case.

Two further caveats. The before and after runs answer different events (`push` and
`pull_request`); the workflow body is identical across the two and both use the same
hosted runners, but they are not the same trigger. And #364's own table estimated ~62s
from a 163s baseline; the suite has grown to 6m10s since those measurements, so the
absolute saving is larger than the issue predicted while the shape of the result is the
same.

The longest job is now `corpus-gates`, not the fast test group #364 predicted would bound
it, so that is where any further workflow-shape work would go.

## Coverage preservation

#364 asks specifically for this: a faster workflow that quietly stopped running a gate
looks identical to a successful optimisation from the outside.

The check replays **both versions of `ci.yml` against a single checkout** and compares
the union of collected pytest node IDs. Every `run:` step that invokes pytest is
extracted from each workflow file and re-run with `--collect-only`, so the only variable
is the workflow edit.

| Tree | Workflow | Unique node IDs |
|---|---|---|
| post-rebase | `develop`'s (pre-split) | 3253 |
| post-rebase | this branch's (post-split) | 3253 |
| pre-rebase | pre-split (`d00b683^`) | 3246 |
| pre-rebase | post-split | 3246 |

Both sets are **identical** within each tree, not merely equal in size: a direct diff of
the sorted node IDs is empty. The check was re-run after the rebase rather than carried
over, since the rebase brings eleven commits of `develop` test changes into the tree and
the earlier result describes a different artifact. The count moves from 3246 to 3253
because `develop` added seven fast tests, and the post-rebase run is the one that matters.

Same-tree replay is what makes that meaningful. An earlier pass compared a collection
taken on `develop` against one taken on this branch, which cannot isolate the split:
this branch is eleven commits behind `develop`, so unrelated test changes land in the
difference alongside the workflow edit. That is also where the earlier note about three
"removed" test modules came from. None of them were removed here. Two
(`test_committed_validation_report.py`, `test_generate_validation_report.py`) are present
on both branches, and `test_browser_skip_guard.py` was **added on `develop`** in `5db1598`
(#599) after this branch was cut.

The comparison was checked against a known-bad case rather than trusted on a green
result. Dropping one module (`tests/test_pdf_watermark_recall.py`) from a copy of the new
workflow made the diff report exactly the one node that module contributes, so an empty
diff means the sets match rather than that the harness read nothing. It read nothing
once, in fact: the first attempt passed `-v` through to `--collect-only`, which outranks
`-q` and prints an indented tree instead of flat node IDs, yielding zero parsed nodes on
both sides. Empty compared equal to empty. The script now strips `-v` and warns when an
invocation yields no nodes.

## Guards

`tests/test_ci_workflow.py` pins the properties the split could silently undo:

| Guard | What it prevents |
|---|---|
| `test_required_test_context_is_an_aggregator_over_all_jobs` | the required `test` context stranding, or reporting green without reading every job's result |
| `test_leaf_jobs_have_no_inter_job_dependencies` | a `needs:` edge between leaf jobs re-serializing what #364 parallelised |
| `test_ci_matrix_jobs_do_not_cancel_sibling_legs` | `fail-fast: true` destroying a sibling leg's verdict |
| `test_ci_matrix_jobs_pin_the_interpreter_they_claim_to_test` | a leg labelled 3.14 silently testing 3.12 |
| `test_required_checks_report_to_a_merge_queue` | a queued pull request waiting forever on a context nothing reports |

Each was verified by injecting its defect into `ci.yml` and confirming the guard goes
red, then restoring.

### Aggregator guard: bind-and-use

The aggregator guard reads one property that is easy to state and easy to get wrong: a
job's result must not merely be *bound* to a variable, it must reach the `for result in`
list that feeds the comparison. A result that is bound and never visited makes the
aggregator a rubber stamp for exactly that one job while every other job still gates,
which is the version of this defect hardest to see in a diff.

An earlier form of the guard searched the whole aggregator script for `$<JOB>_RESULT`
and required each variable to be spelled from its job name. Three cases, run against
both forms:

| Injected into `ci

author: bmethod
body:
## Summary

- Adds `skills/review-gate/references/vendored-paths.md` — the spec for suppressing duplicate consumer-repo findings on vendored vstack paths **without** starving the review gate, plus `templates/vendored-paths.instructions.md`, a paste-in path-scoped reviewer instruction.
- Core rule: **route findings by remedy locus, never silence by path.** Every *configuration* answer (Copilot content exclusion, ignore-paths, path-filtered triggers) removes the vendored tree from the reviewer's view — a pure re-vendor PR then has no reviewable files, so no review object exists and the gate starves at `awaiting`, or a "reviewed 0 files" pass trips `REVIEW_GATE_CHECKRUN_SKIP_PATTERNS`. Instruction text constrains what a reviewer *says*, never *whether it reviews*, so it structurally cannot starve the gate.
- Inline comments stay for repo-owned remedies (the vendor pin, settings, CI wiring); remedies living in the vendored bytes go in the review **summary body** — full evidence, zero threads, zero merge cost.
- Reviewers split into two classes, because they differ in what they can emit: **summary-capable** (Copilot authors a real 1761-char body) and **location-bound** (the Codex connector posts a fixed template body, so its findings can only be inline). The location-bound class gets a bound that fits its actual output contract — one consolidated upstream-remedy comment per PR, not one thread per finding. Per-repo success is therefore "zero Copilot threads and at most one consolidated Codex thread", not zero threads outright.
- Fleet convention documented in `docs/cross-repo.md` ("A Vendored Tree Is Reviewed Once, Upstream"); adoption step 7 + a verification row added to `references/adoption.md`.

## Context

No `REVIEW_GATE_*` value changes. Notably `.agents/*` stays in every consumer's `REVIEW_GATE_CARRY_FORWARD_EXCLUDE` (vendored markdown is mechanically-obeyed agent instruction), and `REVIEW_GATE_TRUSTED_STATUS_CONTEXTS` is not widened to a CI check — a context trusted for this PR class would be trusted for every PR class.

## Completed Issues

- Closes #1242 - Propagation: consumer reviewers skip vendored vstack paths without starving the review-gate evidence

## Measured state — 2026-08-11, the #1235 train

Threads counted via the `reviewThreads` GraphQL read on each repo's open re-vendor PR.

| Repo | Vendored tree | Path-scoped instruction today | Open threads on the #1235 PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| drovr | `.agents/skills/review-gate/**` | present, glob correct | 5 (PR #479) |
| memsira | `.agents/skills/review-gate/**` | present, glob correct | 2 (PR #470) |
| hyprtrade | `tools/review-gate/**` | present, glob correct | 6 (PR #587) |
| hyprtrade-io | `.agents/skills/review-gate/**` | none | 0 (PR #43, merged) |
| vg | `.agents/skills/review-gate/**` | none | 2 (PR #8) |

15 open threads across four consumers, all on vendored paths (Copilot, qodo, Codex connector).

Two findings that shape the rollout:

- **13 of the 15 threads came from the three repos that already carry a vendored-tree instruction.** Their existing clause constrains the *remedy* ("flag them, but do not ask for local edits") and leaves the comment surface alone — which is exactly why it never suppressed anything. Rewriting that clause is the work; adding one where it is missing is the smaller half.
- **hyprtrade-io#43 merged with a Copilot `COMMENTED` review carrying a 1771-char body and zero review threads.** That is the target shape, already observed in production: evidence present, nothing blocking.

## Deviations from the issue's deliverable list

- **No qodo configuration.** qodo drops at trial end (~2026-08-16) and produced roughly a third of the observed threads, so a qodo-side config would be written and retired in the same week. Copilot and the Codex connector are the targets.
- **The per-repo wiring plan is not in this commit.** vstack is portable and public, so the five consumer repo names stay out of tracked files; the filled plan lives untracked at `docs/vendored-review-rollout-local.md` (gitignored via `docs/*-local.md`).
- **`vgs`** was named in the issue but is not one of the five gate-enforcing consumers measured here; whether it vendors a byte-pinned tree at all needs confirming before wiring it.

## Review Round

Three reviewer findings applied in `6fd0c639`:

1. **Location-bound reviewers cannot use a summary body** (codex-connector) — spec and template now split reviewers by class and bound the location-bound class to one consolidated comment per PR. An adapter (new engine machinery) and a summary-capable-only rollout (which would exclude the reviewer producing most of the threads) were both rejected deliberately.
2. **Exact-head verification was unverifiable as documented** (codex-connector) — the command now requests `reviews,headRefOid` and reports `at_head` per review, proven to return both true and false on live PRs (drovr#475 has three reviews at superseded commits; hyprtrade#585 has none at head). Also documents that this view drops the `[bot]` login suffix the trusted-login lists carry.
3. **Skip-pattern protection was overstated** (Copilot) — `REVIEW_GATE_CHECKRUN_SKIP_PATTERNS` is literal-substring `contains()` over title + summary, so a "0 files reviewed" success is full evidence. Both passages corrected; path exclusion risks a hollow **green** gate rather than a starved one, which is the worse failure because nothing looks wrong.

## Test Plan

- 43/43 shell suites pass, 0 fail (the CI shell portion of `skill-tests.yml`: executable-bit lint, `vstack report` guidance lint, orch run-all, all other skill suites, hook suites).
- The doc-contract lint was first proven capable of failing on the new template (an injected `REVIEW_GATE_BOGUS_CONTROL` made `settings-vars-documented.test.sh` fail; removed and re-verified pass) before its pass was trusted.
- Rollout verification is per-repo and out of this PR's reach: five PRs through five separate merge queues, each verified on that repo's own next pure re-vendor PR. Recommended order `hyprtrade → drovr → memsira → vg → hyprtrade-io`, not batched — if the first repo's re-vendor PR starves its gate, the other four are avoided rather than reverted.

author: jackalcooper
body:
## What

Adds a compute capability query to the Zig CUDA runner and exposes it through `Beaver.MLIR.CUDA.device_compute_capability/1`.

## Why

Triton lowering needs the device's compute capability (currently passed explicitly from the target, e.g. `sm_80`). With a runtime query the capability can be derived from the actual device instead of hardcoded targets.

## Changes

- `native/src/cuda_runner.zig`: load `cuDeviceGetAttribute` and add the `cuda_device_compute_capability` NIF returning `{:ok, {major, minor}}` (or `{:error, reason}`)
- `lib/beaver/mlir/capi_handwritten.ex`: register the new raw NIF
- `lib/beaver/mlir/cuda.ex`: public `device_compute_capability/1` API
- `test/cuda_runtime_test.exs`: test the query, with graceful degradation when no CUDA driver is present

## Verification

On this machine (RTX 5070 Laptop): `CUDA.device_compute_capability(0)` returns `{:ok, {12, 0}}`. Without a driver the API returns `{:error, reason}` instead of crashing, matching the existing runner behavior.

body:
# release v0.1.34 — bump acp-kernel to 0.0.19 (fixed 50K nudge growth)

## Summary

Bumps `acp-kernel` from `0.0.18` to **`0.0.19`** and billion-context-pi from
`0.1.33` to **`0.1.34`**. No source changes — billion-context-pi inherits the
kernel's nudge config and bundles it inline (tsup does not mark acp-kernel external).

## What 0.0.19 brings

acp-kernel [v0.0.19](https://github.com/ranxianglei/acp-kernel/pull/61) pins the nudge
growth threshold to a **fixed 50,000 tokens**. Previously `resolveAdaptiveGrowth`
returned `5% of context (clamped 20K–50K)`, so sub-1M-context models got smaller
thresholds and nudges fired too eagerly, driving over-compression. Now every model
uses the same 50K growth threshold.

The change in the kernel (`src/config.ts`):

```diff
- growthFloor: Math.max(20000, Math.round(modelContextLimit * 0.05)),
+ growthFloor: 50000,
```

(`growthCap` is already 50000, so `resolveAdaptiveGrowth` now always returns 50000.)

## Changes in this PR (per AGENTS.md §5 — single release commit, two version fields)

```
"version": "0.1.33" → "0.1.34"
"acp-kernel": "0.0.18" → "0.0.19"
```

Plus `package-lock.json` refreshed against the real 0.0.19 tarball. No source changes.

## Verification

- typecheck (`tsc --noEmit`): clean
- tests (`node --import tsx --test tests/*.test.ts`): 165 pass / 0 fail
- build (`tsup`): success, dist/index.js self-contained (acp-kernel inlined)

## Merge → auto-publish

Merging this PR triggers `release.yml`, which detects the `2026-08-12_release-v*`
branch, tags `v0.1.34`, and publishes to npm `latest`. PR merge is human-only.

Optimizaciones de rendimiento para que la app se sienta instantánea al navegar, abrir modales, filtrar y ejecutar acciones. **Sin cambios de diseño, identidad ni funcionalidades** — cada optimización tiene una razón técnica concreta.

author: lugamafe
body:
Four files. Each one exists because this repository currently misleads
somebody.

## `SECURITY.md` — there was no private channel at all

The only route we offered for a vulnerability was `kensa.ai/report`, which
publishes **immediately and permanently**. Someone who found a token leak and
did the responsible thing would have published a working exploit, with
instructions, under our name.

Private advisories are now **enabled** on this repo, and this file points at
them bluntly — because the mistake cannot be undone. An issue is indexed the
moment it exists, and a screenshot proving the exploit goes to a public bucket
where deleting the issue does **not** delete the file.

## `CONTRIBUTING.md` — the word promises something we cannot deliver

GitHub links this file automatically when someone opens an issue or a PR, so it
is where people look. "CONTRIBUTING" means *here is how to contribute code*, and
the source is private. Its first line disarms that instead of letting the reader
find out the hard way.

It also states the thing that surprises everyone, including us: **an issue filed
through the form is authored by our account.** The reporter is not subscribed
and will never be notified of a reply, a fix, or a close. The URL we hand back
is their only way in. That is now written down where they will see it.

## `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`

Blank issues off, one form on. Only **what happened** is required — a reporter
turned away for lacking reproduction steps is a report lost for good rather than
deferred, because most of them cannot be asked for more later.

The "this becomes public" warning sits **above** the fields. Below the submit
button it would be read by someone who has already pasted their log.

## `.github/pull_request_template.md`

Measured, not assumed: **GitHub does not permit turning forking off on a public
repository.** The API answers `422 — Allow forks setting can only be changed on
org-owned private repositories`. So pull requests can arrive here and there is
nowhere for them to go. Better that a contributor reads why before spending an
evening than after.

## Also applied to this repo (settings, not files)

- Private vulnerability reporting: **enabled**
- Secret scanning + push protection: **enabled** (free on public repos, was off)
- Wiki, Projects: **disabled** — empty tabs and unwatched surfaces
- Rulesets: `main` cannot be deleted or force-pushed; `v*` tags are immutable.
  The tags one matters most — installed auto-updaters read `releases/latest`,
  so a tag deleted by accident points real machines somewhere else.
- **28 labels** replacing a set that included `good first issue` and
  `help wanted` on a repository where nobody can contribute code.

author: hagerox
body:
## Summary

PyTorch checkpoints for RoFormer and MDX23C were loaded with unrestricted pickle deserialization. A malicious checkpoint could therefore execute arbitrary Python code during model conversion.

This PR:

- uses restricted weight-only loading for RoFormer, MDX23C, and VR checkpoints;
- requires PyTorch 2.6 or newer because CVE-2025-32434 affects weight-only loading in earlier releases;
- rejects vulnerable PyTorch versions at runtime before reading a checkpoint;
- adds focused regression coverage for every direct checkpoint loader, including proof that PyTorch 2.5.1 is rejected before `torch.load` runs.

Ordinary tensor state dictionaries and the existing `state_dict`/`model` wrapper formats remain supported. Checkpoints containing arbitrary custom Python objects now fail intentionally.

## Scope

This PR hardens the project's direct RoFormer, MDX23C, and VR checkpoint loaders. It does not change Demucs' upstream model-package loading or the legacy MLX `*_mlx.pkl` cache fallback; that residual work is tracked in #3.

## Security impact

This removes the project's clearest remote-code-execution path when converting downloaded or user-supplied RoFormer, MDX23C, or VR checkpoints.

PyTorch advisory: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/security/advisories/GHSA-53q9-r3pm-6pq6

## Testing

- 224 passed
- 1 skipped
- Targeted Ruff checks passed
- `uv lock --check` passed
- Real PyTorch 2.10 smoke tests confirmed executable pickle payloads are rejected by all three direct loaders

💡 What: Replaced the manual `operator.length` and `operator.charCodeAt(0)` dispatching in `binaryPrecedence` with a direct string `switch(operator)` statement.
🎯 Why: Manual length and character code extraction introduces branching overhead. Modern V8 engines heavily optimize direct string switch blocks for mapping known static strings, eliminating the need for manual performance heuristics.
📊 Impact: Benchmarks demonstrate this direct string switch approach is measurably faster (roughly ~5% faster loop overhead in isolated tests) than the legacy charCode extraction logic.
🔬 Measurement: Run the test suite using `npm test` to verify functionality. Included benchmark script results showed 50M iterations dropped from ~1040ms to ~975ms.

## Summary

DEEP-tier research doc 2264. Exhaustive inventory of what only exists on the Mac, then a per-capability home decision, migration order, and a "what breaks if the Mac is shut for a week" table.

**The finding:** the always-on tier is not missing. The VPS runs 8 services and 22 cron entries, the Pi runs 7 tmux sessions and 7 cron entries, and the VPS already has an authenticated Claude Code install (2.1.167, credentials 2026-08-08). What is missing is reachability and durability:

- The VPS is the ONE machine in the estate not on the tailnet (`which tailscale` returns nothing).
- `~/.zao/` is 292 MB, not a git repo, with one file in `backups/`. It holds the secrets file, the ICM owner keys and 103 transcript directories.
- 74 of 80 `~/bin` tools exist only on the Mac; the VPS has 91 tools the Mac does not. Neither box has the whole toolkit.

Autonomous work survives a week without the Mac. The operator layer does not: 8 Claude lanes, the relay daemon, the capture-to-crush loop, the spend ledger and all 10 MCP servers.

## Two corrections

- `srv1073120` (100.121.237.35) belongs to tailnet user `failoften@`, not `zaalp99@`. Not a ZAO machine to schedule work onto.
- Doc 2262 recorded that the T3 Code upstream repo "did not surface". It exists at `pingdotgg/t3code` and was read directly for this doc: MIT, 18,270 stars, 4,143 forks, 1,611 open issues, `v0.0.34-nightly`. It fits the problem (systemd service, `t3 pair --tailscale`, reuses existing Claude credentials) but only when installed on an always-on box, which requires the tailnet change first. Recommendation is a bounded VPS trial after steps 1-6, nothing gated behind it. Zaal's study-do-not-adopt instruction stands.

## Also found while measuring

The cheap fleet is out of money, not broken. OpenRouter reports `total_credits: 60, total_usage: 60.205736834` - overdrawn by $0.21. `fleet-brain.state` reads `NO_CREDITS`, traced to `fleet-brain-check.sh:22`. Today's loop digest is 602 bytes against 401,482 and 731,140 the two prior days.

## Tier

DEEP. 15 of 15 local measurements FULL, run directly against the Mac, the VPS and the Pi.

## Sources

15 local measurements [FULL] on three machines. `pingdotgg/t3code` repo, README, three docs files, issues and releases APIs [FULL]. HackerNews [FAILED - zero stories on T3 Code, stated rather than substituted]. Reddit [FAILED - fetcher cannot parse a search URL, `.json` route returned 429]. Community coverage is thinner than DEEP normally requires; that is reported in the doc rather than papered over.

10 rows, each with @Zaal as owner, a real date between 2026-08-12 and 2026-09-11, and observable shipped-criteria. Step 1 (`tailscale up` on the VPS, due 2026-08-12) blocks the rest.

Nothing was moved. No service restarted, no lane migrated, no config changed on any box. PR-only per `agent-loops.md` rule 8.

The pre-commit PII scanner flagged a false positive: the T3 nightly version string `20260811.1071` matched the US-phone regex `\d{3}[\s.-]?\d{3}[\s.-]?\d{4}`. I did not bypass it - I dropped the exact build id, which carried no decision weight. Worth a fix, since any version string or timestamp of that shape will trip it.

author: hexiao0225
body:
Everything for the trip in one private app: London → Scotland → the residency, the Beijing side trip, and the flights home to San Mateo.

## What's in it

**One timeline.** Flights, stays, car hire, trains, activities and notes live in a single `segments` table, grouped by day and by leg of the trip. A per-traveler filter covers the stretch where you're in different countries.

**Timezones done properly.** Each segment stores the instant *and* the IANA zone it should be read in. A SFO→LHR leg shows a PDT departure and a BST arrival with the right duration between them, and a red-eye landing at 06:00 in London files under the London date rather than the previous one.

**Email ingestion.** Forward a booking confirmation to a dedicated address and it posts to `/api/inbound/email`. That endpoint normalises Postmark / Resend / SendGrid / Cloudflare payloads, stores the raw mail, acknowledges immediately, then parses in the background with Claude — providers time out in seconds, the model call doesn't.

Two deliberate choices there:

- **Nothing lands on the timeline automatically.** Parsed segments wait in a review queue until confirmed, so a misread never quietly corrupts the itinerary.
- **The raw email is stored before the model runs.** A failed parse keeps the booking and offers a re-parse instead of asking anyone to forward it again.

**Access.** One shared passcode, an HMAC-signed cookie, verified in `proxy.ts` with Web Crypto so it runs on the edge runtime. The webhook is exempt and uses its own shared secret.

## Verified

Against a local Postgres: auth redirect, timeline rendering and timezone conversion, day/leg grouping, per-traveler filter, review queue, segment detail, webhook auth (401s without the token), payload normalisation for Postmark and Resend shapes, and redelivery idempotency. `typecheck`, `lint` and `build` are clean.

**Not verified:** the Claude call itself — there's no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the build environment, so the parse path was only exercised through its failure branch (which correctly recorded the error and surfaced a re-parse button). Worth forwarding one real confirmation after deploying.

## Before it runs

Set the five variables in `.env.example`, then `npm run db:push`. README covers Vercel and getting a free inbound address from Postmark (no domain needed).

`src/lib/config.ts` is the file to edit as plans firm up — traveler names, leg date ranges (mostly TBD), and the countdown milestones.

author: isaacsmithnz-cmyk
body:
> "still says stop and read" — Isaac, 2026-08-10, looking at a recording on prod

Not a stale deploy. The card had **two words for one gesture** — "Stop & read" while the mic is open, "Go" once the words are in the box — and from where the person is standing both are simply the way onward. Recording's button is now Go too, in the same green.

**The square stays.** The word says where you're going; the glyph says what it costs, which is that the recording ends here. A green Go with no stop mark would be the one control on the card giving no sign it's about to close the microphone.

## They are still two different actions

Recording's Go **ends the recording** and shows you the words. Idle's Go **commits** them. Sharing a name is safe only because they never share a screen — one exists while the mic is open, the other only once there's something to sort — and that assumption is pinned along with the rest.

If a later tidy-up ever crosses the handlers, the labels will still look right while the card files a note nobody has read. That's the exact failure "speaking does not commit" was built to prevent, so `note-token-go.test.tsx` asserts recording's Go calls `stop` and never `routeNote`.

## The error in the screenshot

"Nothing was said in that one. Try again, or type it." was still on the card **six seconds into the recording it had just invited** — a message that asks for a retry, then calls the retry a failure before the first sentence is out. And "that one" had come to point at a recording the person could see running.

An error belongs to the attempt that produced it, so pressing the mic retires it. Wrapped in the flow rather than in `useDictation`: the engine *reports* errors, it doesn't own them, and every posture goes through `flow.dict`.

Both halves are tested — a new recording clears the last one's error, and an error the current attempt produced stays put. Clearing on any old render would make a failure flash and vanish, which is indistinguishable from the app ignoring you.

## Verification

Both Go buttons measured against the real stylesheet in the static harness: identical `linear-gradient(120deg,#00E5C0,#00A389)`, with `Save these` still teal→blue. Six new tests; **5,147 jest tests green**, typecheck and lint clean.

One environment note: `npx tsc` and `src/lib/tiff/__tests__/ocr.test.ts` were both failing on `Cannot find module 'pdf-lib'` — #339 declared it in `package.json` but this machine's `node_modules` predated it. Fixed with `npm install --no-save pdf-lib` (nothing committed); CI installs from the manifest and was never affected.

**Still not walked signed-in.** The capture card is behind auth and previews can't sign in, so the labels and the error lifecycle are jest-and-harness verified only.

author: momiah
body:
Prerequisite for connecting **courtchamps-website** (and later the mobile app) to this package.

## Why
- CRA (`react-scripts`) forces `moduleResolution: "node"` (classic). Under classic resolution TypeScript **ignores the `exports` map**, so `import … from "courtchamps-shared/types"` fails to resolve the shipped `.d.ts` (verified: TS emits `TS2307 … consider updating to 'node16'/'nodenext'/'bundler'`).

## What
- Add a `typesVersions` map for `/types`, `/schema`, `/helpers` → their `dist/*.d.ts`, so classic-resolution consumers resolve types. Modern-resolution consumers keep using the `exports` conditions unchanged.

## Verification
- With a CRA-style tsconfig (`module: esnext`, `moduleResolution: node`), a consumer importing `courtchamps-shared/types` fails without this change and type-checks cleanly with it (confirmed the `typesVersions` block ships in the packed tarball).
